opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important dynamics to understand right now. The simplest version is that our own engineers use Claude every day to write code. A large and growing share of the code going into our systems is drafted by the model, with humans reviewing and steering. That alone compounds: if each researcher gets meaningfully more done, you run more experiments, you find what works faster, and that feeds into the next model.

It goes beyond coding, though. The models help with evals, data generation, debugging training runs, and analyzing results. Constitutional AI was an early version of this: instead of having humans label every example of what's harmful or helpful, you have the model critique and revise its own outputs against a set of principles. That scales much better than pure human feedback, and it's a template for using AI to supervise and improve AI.

Where it gets interesting, and a bit sobering, is when the loop tightens. Today a human is still in the loop at almost every step, deciding what to try, interpreting results, making judgment calls. But you can see the trajectory where the model is doing more of the research itself, proposing ideas, running them, and iterating. If that happens, progress could speed up a lot, possibly faster than our institutions or our safety techniques are ready for.

That's a big part of why we care so much about things like our Responsible Scaling Policy. One of the capability thresholds we watch closely is autonomous AI research ability, because that's where you could get a really steep curve. We want to be measuring it carefully, have safeguards in place before we cross it, and make sure alignment and interpretability research benefits from the same acceleration. Ideally the AI that helps build better models also helps us understand and trust those models. That's the bet: use the acceleration to make safety go faster too, not just capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's honestly the biggest driver of how fast things are moving right now.

The simplest version is that the models are already writing a huge fraction of the code at Anthropic. I'd say most engineers on the research side are using Claude Code for the majority of what they do day to day. So the pace at which we can try experiments, build infrastructure, debug training runs, fix flaky evals, all of that has gotten dramatically faster. And a lot of what research actually is, is iteration speed. If you can run twice as many experiments in the same amount of time, you learn twice as fast about what works.

But I think the more interesting piece is the stuff that's a little harder to see from the outside. A lot of the work of training a model is pretty unglamorous. It's data pipelines, it's cleaning things up, it's figuring out why a job fell over at three in the morning. Models are getting really good at that kind of long-horizon, grindy engineering work, where the task is well specified but there are a thousand little steps. That frees people up to think about the questions where human judgment still matters a lot, like what should we even be trying to do, and how do we know if we've succeeded.

Then there's the research itself. Models are increasingly good at generating hypotheses, reading the literature, proposing ablations, even writing up results. We're not at the point where you can just say "go make the next model better" and walk away. But we are at the point where a researcher with a model is a very different kind of researcher than one without. It's a bit like having a team of very fast, very eager grad students who never sleep.

And I think the thing that people underestimate is that this compounds. Every generation of model is better at helping build the next one. The model we have today helped build itself in a meaningful sense, and the one after that will have even more of its development done with AI in the loop. That's why we take the timelines seriously. When I look at where this goes, you end up with something that looks like a country of geniuses in a data center, and the main constraint becomes compute and how carefully you want to move, not how many smart people you can hire.

Which is also, frankly, why safety work has to keep pace. If the feedback loop is getting tighter, you want to be very confident about what's in that loop. We spend a lot of time making sure the models that are helping us do research are aligned and honest, because errors there don't stay small for long. So I'm optimistic, but it's an optimism that comes with a lot of responsibility attached.

astra-6.text:
I think the first step is AI making researchers and engineers more productive—helping write code, debug experiments, and understand results. You still have humans deciding what questions matter, but you can test more ideas in the same amount of time.

The more interesting step is when models can participate in that research loop: propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, and use the results to decide what to try next. If that works reliably, improvements to a model could help accelerate the development of its successor.

But I wouldn’t assume that automatically produces an instantaneous takeoff. You still have constraints like compute, how long experiments take, and how well you can tell whether an apparent improvement is real. The key question is how much of the research process models can actually do—and whether they can do the parts that are holding progress back.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest shift comes when models can help with the research process itself. Today, a researcher has an idea, writes some code, runs an experiment, looks at the results, and decides what to try next. Models can already help with pieces of that. As they get more capable, they can take on longer stretches of that loop.

The interesting threshold isn’t just writing the code faster. It’s being able to suggest a useful experiment, recognize when a result is surprising, and figure out what that tells you about your original hypothesis. If you can do that reliably, you can explore a lot more ideas in parallel.

I don’t think that automatically means you get an instantaneous intelligence explosion. You still have experiments that take time, compute constraints, and the difficulty of knowing whether something is actually an improvement. But it could substantially shorten the cycle between one generation of models and the next. And that makes evaluating and understanding those improvements increasingly important.
